transcript.text: Bosch KGN34NL3AG - some days it's fine, other days it just clicks every few minutes at the back and doesn't seem to run, and the freezer starts getting soft. Then it starts working again by itself. What's going on?

## What's Probably Happening

That pattern (a click every few minutes from the back, no running hum, freezer softening, then it recovers on its own) almost always means the compressor is trying to start and failing. The click is usually one of these:

1. The compressor's overload protector tripping (most common). The fridge tries to start the compressor, it draws too much current or gets too hot, and a thermal cut-out clicks off. It cools down for a few minutes, clicks back on, tries again, and fails again. Eventually it succeeds and runs normally for a while.
2. A failing start relay / PTC starter on the side of the compressor. This is a cheap part that wears out and causes exactly this intermittent behaviour.
3. A fault in the compressor's electronic control board. Many recent Bosch models use variable-speed (inverter) compressors with a small control board mounted at the compressor. When that board or the compressor is failing, you get repeated start attempts and clicking.
4. The compressor itself is wearing out. Hard starting that comes and goes can be an early sign of this.

## Things Worth Checking Yourself

These are the causes you can rule out without any tools:

• Extension leads and adaptors: Plug it directly into a wall socket. Low or unstable voltage makes compressors struggle to start.
• Ventilation: Make sure there's a gap behind and above the unit and nothing is blocking airflow. An overheated compressor trips its overload far more easily.
• Room temperature: Problems that show up on warm days, or in a hot garage or utility room, point to heat-related tripping.
• Feel the compressor (the black dome at the bottom back) during a clicking phase. If it's very hot and clicking without humming, that confirms the overload is cutting it out.
• Note the timing. Clicks roughly every 2–5 minutes are typical of an overload/start problem, which is useful info for an engineer.

## What to Do

• Check your warranty. This is the first thing to do. Bosch appliances often come with at least 2 years' cover, and some compressor-related faults have extended cover. Your receipt or the Bosch website (register/check with the serial number from the label inside the fridge) will tell you. Bosch Home UK service can book an engineer.
• If it's out of warranty, a refrigeration engineer can test the start relay and overload, which are cheap fixes. If it turns out to be the compressor or inverter board, get a quote and weigh it against the age of the fridge. Compressor replacement on a sealed system is often not economical on an older unit.
• Protect your food in the meantime. Freezer food that has softened but still has ice crystals can usually be refrozen. Anything fully thawed (especially meat and fish) should be cooked or used, not refrozen. A cheap fridge/freezer thermometer helps you keep track.

Don't leave this too long. Repeated failed starts put a lot of stress on the compressor, so a cheap relay problem can turn into an expensive compressor failure.

Thank you, that's helpful. To answer your checks: it's plugged directly into the wall socket, there's a gap behind it though the back is a bit dusty, and the compressor is very hot to the touch when it's clicking. There's no burning smell and nothing has tripped. The fridge is about 10 years old, so it's well out of warranty. What would you suggest as the next step?

A very hot compressor that clicks without humming confirms the compressor is trying to start and its overload protector is cutting it out. The good news is that there's one cheap thing to try first, and the dust may be part of the problem.

## Step 1: Clean the Back (Free, Worth Doing First)

Dust traps heat around the compressor and condenser, making it run hotter and harder to start.

1. Unplug the fridge and pull it out carefully.
2. Vacuum the back, especially around the compressor at the bottom and any coils, grille, or small fan down there. A soft brush attachment works well.
3. Leave it unplugged for at least 15-30 minutes so the compressor cools fully. Move frozen food to a cool box or a neighbour's freezer if possible.
4. Plug it back in and listen. A healthy start is a click followed by a steady hum, not a click and silence.
5. Push it back with a decent gap, ideally several centimetres at the back, and keep the top clear.

Then watch it for a few days, ideally with a cheap fridge/freezer thermometer. If the clicking episodes stop or become much rarer, overheating was the main factor.

## Step 2: If It Keeps Happening

The likely causes, roughly from cheapest to most expensive:

• Start relay / PTC starter or overload protector: a small plug-on part on the side of the compressor. It's often inexpensive and replaceable without touching the refrigerant. This only applies if your model has a conventional compressor rather than an inverter type, which a technician can confirm quickly.
• Inverter control module: if fitted, it costs more but is still sometimes worth replacing.
• Failing compressor: replacing it means cutting into the sealed system, which requires an F-gas certified engineer. On a 10-year-old fridge this usually costs as much as or more than a new fridge, so it rarely makes financial sense.

My suggestion: if cleaning doesn't fix it, have an engineer diagnose it and ask for a quote before any work. If it's the relay or starter, repair is worthwhile. If it's the compressor, put the money towards a replacement. A modern fridge freezer will also use noticeably less electricity than a 10-year-old one.

## In the Meantime: Food Safety

• The freezer should be -18°C or colder. Check it during and after a bad spell.
• Food that has partly thawed but still has ice crystals can usually be refrozen.
• Food that has fully thawed, especially meat and fish, should be cooked and eaten, or cooked and then refrozen, not refrozen raw.
• If in doubt, throw it out, particularly if it's been above 5°C for a few hours.

If the episodes become more frequent or last longer, that suggests the problem is worsening. That's a good cue to make the repair-or-replace decision before you lose a full freezer load.
